title: AMD stock plunges after short-seller says the chip maker has its own China problems - Business Insider
content: Nvidia is no longer the only US chip giant in the crosshairs of bearish short-sellers. AMD stock plunged as much as 11% on Thursday after Hunterbrook revealed a short position pegged to claims that the company may have business ties to IEIT Systems, a Chinese IT firm blacklisted by the US government in March 2025. Shares closed down about 8%. "Over a year and a half later, on October 19, 2026, IEIT posted a software update for one of its AMD servers," the short report said. "Hunterbrook Media downloaded the file and found AMD's code inside: the startup firmware that AMD writes for its chips, in a version issued after the blacklisting." They also flagged AMD's relationship with Aivres, a company identified as a key part of Nvidia's Chinese business network. The report comes after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid controversy related to extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang's ties to Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive, were first flagged by short-seller Culper Research in May, and reported on by the New York Times at the end of October. This week, Muddy Waters also revealed a bet against Nvidia, highlighting ties between former Nvidia exec Jay Puri and Cenly Chen, a former executive at Super Micro Computer, later reported by The Information to be his wife. Now, Hunterbrook sees problems with China ties looming over one of Nvidia's biggest rivals. Both companies are facing the threat of stricter export controls that could take effect in January, and AMD is "no less at risk from China chip restrictions," than Nvidia. The team behind the short repor noted that AMD may be highly exposed to China, adding that the company did not respond to questions it had about its business. "The trouble is that AMD's growth story rests on the chips that face tighter restrictions," the report stated. "The company has told investors it aims to grow data center AI revenue by more than 80% a year over the next three to five years, chasing a market Nvidia dominates." An AMD spokesperson issued the following statement to Business Insider regarding the claims in Hunterbrook's report: Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters. "The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships. AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."

title: Trump's Hints at China Blackwell Nvidia Chip Sales, Yet NVDA Stock Breaks Below $150 Post Earnings, as Elon Musk Criticizes Nvidia Board for Ousting Jensen Huang - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia delivered another record quarter, beating expectations and forecasting $130 billion in fourth-quarter revenue. But, NVDA stock surrendered the initial rally above $160 and fallen below $150 as investors weigh potential Blackwell sales to China, regulatory scrutiny, short-seller allegations, leadership uncertainty and growing resistance to data-centre expansion. Nvidia shares have struggled to sustain their post-earnings momentum despite exceptional financial results, with renewed uncertainty surrounding China’s access to its advanced processors adding pressure. Speaking to Fox News from Shenzhen following his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, President Trump suggested that Blackwell sales to China could become possible in two or three years, by which time Nvidia would have moved further ahead technologically. Blackwell is Nvidia’s previous-generation computing platform, with its successor, Vera Rubin, now entering the market. During the November 17 earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress described Vera Rubin as the fastest product ramp in Nvidia’s history. The prospect of eventually reopening the Chinese market could provide another significant revenue opportunity. However, export restrictions and geopolitical tensions remain obstacles, while allowing China access to older-generation processors could become less commercially attractive as Nvidia advances its product roadmap. Nvidia initially rallied above $160 following its fiscal Q3 2027 results but subsequently reversed, falling below $150 despite beating expectations across major financial metrics. Revenue reached a record $115.8 billion, increasing 103% year over year and 20.3% sequentially. Adjusted EPS came in at $2.68, above analyst expectations of $2.47, while net income climbed to approximately $65.3 billion. Management also delivered an exceptionally strong fourth-quarter revenue forecast of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, compared with consensus expectations of approximately $124.4 billion. Data Center revenue reached $107.6 billion, exceeding forecasts of $101.87 billion and accounting for approximately 93% of total revenue. Hyperscale customers contributed $60.1 billion, while AI cloud, industrial and enterprise customers generated another $47.5 billion. Adjusted gross margin stood at 74.9%. Nvidia also authorised an additional $150 billion in share repurchases, taking remaining buyback capacity to approximately $227.3 billion. Nevertheless, the concentration of revenue in Data Center exposes Nvidia to any slowdown in infrastructure spending by major cloud providers. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have attempted the upside again and above $233 last month as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers were not able to sustain the rally and we saw dive below $150 today, with NVDA braking the last support at the 100 weekly SMA in green this week. But buyer are attempting to make a comeback pushing the stock above $164. Regulatory and disclosure concerns have added another layer of uncertainty. Nvidia did not submit its quarterly Form 10-Q alongside its earnings announcement, with management indicating that the filing would follow in the coming weeks. The Wall Street Journal has also reported that the SEC is investigating whether Nvidia’s investor disclosures were misleading. No wrongdoing has been established. Meanwhile, short seller Muddy Waters disclosed a position against Nvidia, raising questions about alleged connections involving former executives and the distribution of Nvidia-powered equipment amid investigations into potential illegal exports to China. These allegations remain unproven. Leadership uncertainty and reported succession discussions have further complicated the investment outlook. However, claims surrounding Jensen Huang’s reported departure and potential successors require independent confirmation and should not be treated as established corporate developments without an official Nvidia announcement. Meanwhile, opposition to data-centre construction is increasing across Texas, Ohio and Georgia. Concerns about electricity prices, grid capacity and water consumption could delay projects, increase infrastructure costs and force hyperscalers to reconsider expansion plans. Nvidia’s record earnings and strong forward guidance demonstrate that demand for its processors remains substantial. However, the reversal below $150 suggests investors are becoming less willing to reward growth without considering the risks surrounding customer concentration, geopolitical restrictions and infrastructure spending. With Blackwell potentially facing a longer-term opportunity in China, the transition toward Vera Rubin and continued expansion of Data Center remain important growth catalysts. Nevertheless, further regulatory complications or a slowdown in hyperscaler capital expenditure could expose the stock to renewed selling pressure. Ultimately, Nvidia’s challenge is no longer simply demonstrating demand, but convincing investors that extraordinary growth can continue at a scale that justifies its valuation.

title: Is Nvidia Stock a Once-in-a-Decade Buying Opportunity After Its Latest Earnings? - The Motley Fool
content: There is a light at the end of the tunnel for Nvidia. By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 19, 2026 at 4:15PM EST The past week has been hard on Nvidia (NVDA -3.30%). The semiconductor leader had to separate from its co-founder and now-former CEO, Jensen Huang, after he was embroiled in a scandal involving alleged extramarital affairs, including with a woman believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Colette Kress, who remains CFO, has stepped up as interim CEO, leading the company through its first quarterly update since Huang's departure. And what an update it was. Nvidia once again crushed expectations, but that wasn't enough to jolt the stock, which remains down significantly since it reached a new all-time high in early October. Is Nvidia a generational buying opportunity at current levels? Death, taxes, and Nvidia's financial results coming in above analysts' projections seem to be the only certain things these days. In the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which ended on Oct. 25, the company's revenue came in at $115.8 billion, up 103% compared to the year-ago period. Data center revenue grew 110% year over year to $107.6 billion. Nvidia's non-GAAP gross margin was 74.9%, compared to the 73.5% reported in the prior-year quarter. The semiconductor specialist's non-GAAP operating income was $77.9 billion, rising 116% year over year, while its non-GAAP earnings per share were $2.68, up 111% year over year. The fact that profits are growing faster than revenue is a strong sign for Nvidia, given the industry's increasing competitiveness. While some investors worry that competition from custom AI chips will erode the company's pricing power in the GPU (graphics processing unit) market, as hyperscalers and other corporations increasingly opt for these custom chips, it seems, at least, that this hasn't happened yet. Improving margins are a sign that Nvidia maintains strong pricing power. Meanwhile, Nvidia's free cash flow for the period was $43.8 billion, rising 98% year over year. The company also posted excellent guidance. Nvidia expects $130 billion in revenue (at the midpoint) for its fourth quarter. That would represent a 91% year-over-year increase. Of course, Nvidia's financial results and guidance were only part of the story. The market wants to know how the company's efforts to replace Huang are going. Nvidia said it isn't interested in bringing back Huang, despite many people, both inside and outside the company, calling for his reinstatement. And it is actively looking for a replacement, although nobody knows when Nvidia will find someone to step into the CEO role permanently. In my opinion, that's both good and bad. It's bad because the longer this search drags on, the more uncertainty it could add to the company's prospects. But it's good because replacing a CEO as effective as Huang isn't an easy task, and the company's board is rightfully taking the time it needs to do so, or so it seems. In the meantime, several factors highlight just how massive an opportunity Nvidia could still tap into, even as it faces a more stringent regulatory environment. During the recent U.S. midterm elections, voters elected many lawmakers and politicians across various states who had promised to be stricter on the AI industry. This may result in delayed permits and slower data center build-outs. However, Nvidia expects a great year ahead. The company raised its guidance for the fiscal year 2028, which covers most of the calendar year 2027. The company now expects revenue to grow 75% in fiscal year 2028, up from its previous projection of 70% -- and that's after also raising its guidance for its current fiscal year. If we assume Nvidia's fourth-quarter revenue lands at the midpoint, it could generate $423.7 billion this fiscal year and $741.4 billion next year, based on its projected 75% growth rate. So, given its current market cap of $3.8 trillion, Nvidia is trading at 5.1x estimated fiscal year 2028 revenue -- that's more than fair for a company growing as fast as it is, in my view. However, the CEO search does introduce some uncertainty. And we still have to account for the risk of margin erosion as industry competition intensifies. So, what's the verdict? Nvidia looks like a buy at current levels, but it's hardly a once-in-a-decade buying opportunity. title: Nvidia's (NASDAQ: NVDA) $390 Billion Memory Stockpile Deepens Apple's (NASDAQ: AAPL) Margin Crisis Through 2027 - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 19, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) has locked up $390 billion in supply commitments, up $111 billion from just three months earlier, with the bulk of that increase tied to multi-year memory procurement deals. The scale of that buying spree sits at the center of a deepening cost crisis for device manufacturers, none more exposed than Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), which is already watching its margins contract sharply. Apple’s gross margin fell from 50.1% in the June quarter to 47.9% in September, and the company guided its December quarter to a range of just 45% to 46%. Stripping out tariff refunds that flattered both periods, the adjusted decline runs from roughly 48.1% to 46.9%, with the December guide marking a further step down. Apple CFO Kevan Parekh has said memory alone accounted for more than the entire drop in the company’s adjusted gross margin, a striking admission of how concentrated the pressure is. Outgoing CEO Tim Cook described the pricing environment in blunter terms, calling it “a 100-year flood on the memory pricing” during what was his final earnings call in that role. Investor and media personality Josh Brown, speaking on The Compound and Friends podcast, argued that if Nvidia pulled back on memory purchasing after Jensen Huang’s announced departure on Nov. 12, Apple would stand to benefit most, stating: “There is no greater beneficiary than Apple and its pricing power and its need for that same memory for its own devices.” Nvidia’s own November 17 CFO commentary delivered a direct rebuttal to that thesis, revealing the $390 billion commitment figure and confirming the deals were signed while Huang was still in the chief executive role. Roughly $203 billion of those commitments falls within Nvidia’s fiscal 2028, which closes in January of that year, meaning memory market competition from Nvidia peaks precisely when Apple’s analysts are projecting a margin recovery. Wall Street currently expects Apple’s earnings per share to grow around 5% in fiscal 2027 before accelerating to approximately 12% in fiscal 2028, a rebound that assumes memory costs begin easing in time to help results. Apple has already tried to pass some costs on to consumers, with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max each priced $100 higher than their predecessors, following similar increases on MacBook models in June, though the company has acknowledged those hikes only partially offset the memory burden. Micron (NASDAQ: MU) sits on the other side of the trade as a clear winner, with analysts forecasting its revenue to more than double in fiscal 2027 to $276 billion, after an estimated tripling in fiscal 2026. HP (NYSE: HPQ), which carries far less pricing leverage than Apple, offers a cautionary parallel, with its PC unit volume falling 16% in its most recent quarter even as revenue rose 18%, and its PC operating margin thinning from 5.4% to 4.6%. Much of Nvidia’s memory demand is for high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators, but that product is built on stacked DRAM fabricated from the same underlying wafer capacity that Apple and other device makers compete for. Any genuine relief on Apple’s gross margin likely remains a 2028 story at the earliest, and even that projection carries risk if Nvidia’s new leadership decides to maintain rather than unwind its predecessor’s aggressive procurement posture. Ewan is a reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, primarily covering US current affairs and news related to NYSE-listed stocks. He has over two decades of experience in journalism and digital publishing.

title: 4 Things the Headlines Missed in Nvidia's First Post-Jensen Earnings Report - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia easily beat third-quarter expectations, yet the real story is hiding in the fine print. Interim CEO Colette Kress just dialed back the sales swagger and put customer financing on a tighter leash. The leather jacket is gone, and the spreadsheets are officially in charge. Reporting its first quarterly results just days after former CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation, Nvidia (NVDA -3.30%) proved that its AI dominance doesn't depend on one charismatic ringmaster. In Q3 of fiscal year 2027, Nvidia's revenue soared 103% year over year to $115.8 billion, the new Vera Rubin architecture racked up nearly $20 billion in sales in its debut quarter, and interim CEO Colette Kress even raised the company's fiscal 2028 revenue growth target from 70% to 75%. But beneath those breathtaking headline numbers, interim CEO Colette Kress delivered the report with the measured calm you expect from a 13-year veteran CFO. Kress toned down some of her predecessor's boldest growth framing while tightening the guardrails around how Nvidia deploys its capital. It's a serious top-level strategy shift, brought on by an unexpected scandal. You can see most of it in the earnings release and prepared CFO comments without even digging into the earnings call. And I think I like Kress's attitude. For the first time in forever, Nvidia's business plan makes sense to me. Back in the second quarter, Nvidia couldn't resist hyping up its $105 billion lease guarantee for OpenAI's massive Ohio AI data center campus, telling investors that each generation of chips installed there could generate $150 billion to $200 billion in Nvidia revenue. When the Total Conviction signal flashed for Nvidia in 2009, most people ignored it. The ones who acted turned $5,000 into $2,799,718*. Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. In her debut quarter at the helm, Kress deleted that $200 billion sales pitch from the report. Instead, she offered a step-by-step breakdown of how Nvidia's credit guarantee will take effect across nine separate buildings starting in fiscal year 2029. She also reassured investors by noting that Nvidia hasn't yet paid out any of its financing guarantees. The expected growth is still record-breaking, but on a scale from 1 to 10, Kress dialed back the marketing swagger from 11 to 6. A longtime CFO could be expected to starve Nvidia's growth engine in order to hoard cash. The supply chain numbers say that Nvidia will have plenty of growth fuel under new management. Kress lifted Nvidia's multi-year supply and memory chip commitments from $279 billion in Q2 to $390 billion in Q3. The boost springs from incredible demand for the Vera Rubin AI accelerator. Where did she tighten things up? That would be in the customer financing area. Reported additional commitments related to cash-burning "neocloud" start-ups fell from $56 billion to $32 billion. A new warning in the reporting boilerplate said that those commitments can be "reduced or eliminated" if the neoclouds fail to line up their own financing. And on the call, Kress noted that the underlying deal terms haven't changed; Nvidia will simply be "disciplined and selective" about these contracts. Non-investment-grade customers had better have their capital and end buyers lined up before Nvidia commits to shipping them GPUs from a scarce supply. To gauge Nvidia's financial health, Wall Street spends hours and hours analyzing the capital spending budgets of Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta Platforms. Hyperscalers are no longer the fastest-growing part of the business, though. And they may soon become the smaller slice, too. Hyperscale revenue climbed 71% year over year to $60.1 billion, but Nvidia's AI Clouds, Industrial, and Enterprise segment roughly tripled. Sales in this segment jumped 195% to $47.5 billion. The roster of non-tech-giant customers is broadening fast, including sovereign AI initiatives, enterprise quantitative trading clusters, and stand-alone Vera CPU sales. Nvidia guided fourth-quarter revenue to $130 billion, up from $115.8 billion in Q3. That's a massive number, but it comes with a big calendar footnote: the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2027 includes 14 weeks instead of the 13 seen in most quarters. That's how the cookie crumbles when there are 52 weeks and one day in a non-leap year (and another leap day roughly every four years). With Nvidia currently ringing up nearly $10 billion in sales every week, that extra calendar week accounts for more than 60% of the sequential revenue jump between Q3 and Q4. The underlying demand for Nvidia's AI silicon is definitely strong. Still, investors should remember that the calendar is giving Q4 a temporary tailwind this year -- and next year's 13-week fourth quarter will face the same calendar quirk in reverse. title: SpaceX Is Now Nvidia's Biggest Stock Holding, Ahead of Intel. Here's What That Says About SpaceX. - The Motley Fool
content: Is the chipmaker actually betting more on the rocket and AI company? 10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies › Nvidia (NVDA -3.30%) filed its quarterly list of stock holdings on Monday, Nov. 16, and there's a new name on top. As of Sept. 30, SpaceX (SPCX -3.53%) was the chipmaker's biggest disclosed stake, worth around $19.7 billion, or 40.7% of the reported portfolio. Intel (INTC +1.92%), which led the list three months before, slid to second with 40.1%. Nvidia owned around 130.5 million SpaceX shares at the end of September, up from about 122.8 million at the end of June. Meanwhile, it shrank its Intel stake by a quarter, to around 161.1 million shares. Intel's still the bigger holding by share count. SpaceX leads in value. It's tempting to take this as Nvidia betting more on SpaceX. But I think the filing says less about that than it seems -- and more about how much SpaceX's own plans rely on Nvidia. The filing (a Form 13F, the quarterly holdings report big investment managers send regulators) lists positions on one date. It doesn't say why a position changed. And Nvidia had a way to get more SpaceX shares without buying any. It invested in artificial intelligence (AI) coding firm Cursor in late 2025. SpaceX later bought Cursor in a deal that closed on Aug. 14, paying Cursor's shareholders in SpaceX stock. Some or all of the 7.7 million or so extra shares may have come from the deal. Neither company has said. The bigger shift was on the Intel side. Nvidia's SpaceX stake lost value in the third quarter, dipping from around $21 billion to $19.7 billion as SpaceX's share price dropped. But its Intel stake fell far more, from around $30 billion to $19.4 billion, after Nvidia cut its position by about 54 million shares and Intel's share price slid. Without the extra SpaceX shares, Intel would still have barely kept the top spot. In other words, SpaceX rose to first mainly because Nvidia shrank its Intel stake. For SpaceX, the stake's small. Nvidia's 130.5 million shares made up about 1% of the 13.6 billion or so SpaceX had outstanding in mid-October. At roughly $141 a share as I write, they're worth about $18 billion, versus a market value of about $1.9 trillion. They don't come with much say, either. At the June initial public offering (IPO), CEO Elon Musk had about 82% of the total voting power. The more important tie runs the other way. SpaceX is a big buyer of Nvidia's chips, and its fastest-growing business relies on them. Showing how quickly that business is scaling, SpaceX's super intelligence (SI) segment (its AI cloud services, Grok, Cursor, and X) grew revenue to around $7.6 billion in the third quarter. That's nearly triple the second quarter's $2.6 billion and over nine times the $813 million it took in a year earlier. And the segment swung to $431 million of operating income after losing around $1.3 billion in the second quarter. Its nameplate computing capacity (a measure of the AI chips it's installed) hit 1.7 gigawatts at the end of September, against 1.4 in June and 0.6 in September 2025. Most of SpaceX's capital spending now goes into this build-out. SI took $16.4 billion of the company's third-quarter capital expenditures, or around 84%. "We're tracking to be able to bring roughly 200,000 GB300s online per month for every month for the remainder of this year," Musk said on SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call on Oct. 20. The GB300 is one of Nvidia's AI systems, and Musk said next year's build would be mainly Nvidia's newer Vera Rubin platform. Also, SpaceX's prospectus said its compute deal with Anthropic, which agreed to pay $1.25 billion a month through May 2029, includes around 325,000 Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs). Of course, Nvidia does fine either way. It makes money when SpaceX buys chips, whether or not those chips end up paying off for SpaceX shareholders. What does Nvidia's filing say about SpaceX, then? Not that the chipmaker is making a big new bet. The stake is around 1% of the company, and it might have grown in the Cursor deal. What it does show is how tightly SpaceX's growth is tied to one supplier's products. At around 33 times the revenue SpaceX would bring in over a year at its third-quarter rate, the stock already assumes those chips pay off. I don't find anything in Nvidia's filing that makes the stock look cheaper. When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. title: Nvidia (NVDA Stock) Posts Record $115.8 Billion Revenue as AI Boom Raises Emissions Concerns - CarbonCredits.com
content: Nvidia has reported record quarterly revenue of US$115.8 billion, more than doubling its sales from a year earlier as demand for artificial intelligence (AI) chips continues to grow. The results beat Wall Street estimates and came with a stronger outlook for the next quarter, showing that spending on AI infrastructure remains strong. However, the earnings report also arrives during a major leadership crisis. Co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO and board member on November 12. During its November 17 earnings call, Nvidia’s board confirmed that it does not intend to reinstate him. Beyond its financial growth, Nvidia faces another challenge: managing the rising environmental impact of AI. Its latest sustainability report shows a sharp increase in supply chain emissions, even as the company matches all its operational electricity use with clean energy. This raises questions about whether its climate targets can keep pace with the rapid expansion of AI computing. Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended October 25. This was a 103% increase from $57 billion a year earlier and 20% higher than the previous quarter. Net income rose 105% year-over-year to $65.3 billion. Earnings per diluted share reached $2.70 on a GAAP basis, up 108% from $1.30 in the same quarter last year. Non-GAAP earnings per share climbed 111% to $2.68. The company’s data center business remained the main growth driver. Revenue from this segment reached $107.6 billion, up 110% from a year earlier. It accounted for about 93% of total quarterly sales, reflecting strong demand for AI processors and computing systems. Nvidia also reported a gross margin of 74.8% on a GAAP basis. This was slightly below the 75% recorded in the previous quarter but above the 73.4% reported a year earlier. The company returned $28.1 billion to shareholders through share buybacks and dividends during the quarter. It also had $227.3 billion remaining under its share repurchase authorization at the end of the period. These results show how quickly Nvidia has grown as companies invest in AI data centers and computing infrastructure. However, the scale of its dependence on data center demand also makes the company sensitive to any slowdown in AI spending. Colette Kress, interim CEO and Executive VP and CFO of Nvidia, remarked: “Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people. Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater.” Nvidia expects fourth-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue to reach $130 billion, with a possible range of $126.1 billion to $133.9 billion. This is above the market’s average forecast of just over $125 billion. The outlook is notable because Nvidia said it does not expect any data center computing revenue from China during the quarter. This suggests that demand from other markets could support its growth even without sales to China. Interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress also told investors that Nvidia expects revenue to grow 75% in fiscal 2028. The company has begun shipping its new Vera Rubin NVL72 computing systems, which it described as the fastest product ramp in its history. Still, investors must consider the leadership change. Huang resigned on November 12 after the company disclosed that his personal conduct was inconsistent with its code of conduct and workplace standards. The board unanimously accepted his resignation and appointed Kress as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. The issue became more significant on November 17, when Huang publicly said he would be honored to return if the board believed it was in the company’s best interest. However, board chair Harvey C. Jones said during the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate him. Nvidia also said it would not take questions about Huang’s resignation during the call. The board has formed a committee to oversee national security and export-control issues, adding another layer of scrutiny to the company’s governance. Nvidia (NVDA) stock gained about 5% in after-hours trading on November 17 following the earnings release, as investors welcomed the stronger-than-expected revenue forecast and improved growth outlook. The rebound came after the stock had fallen roughly 10% since Huang’s resignation, reflecting concerns about the leadership change and its potential impact on the company. Despite the leadership turmoil, Nvidia’s results suggest that its business remains strong. However, the search for a permanent CEO will test whether the company can maintain its product roadmap, customer relationships, and growth without its longtime leader. Nvidia’s financial growth reflects the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure. Still, more powerful computing systems also require more electricity, cooling, and materials. The company’s fiscal 2026 sustainability report shows that its total reported Scope 3 emissions reached 10.7 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (MtCO2e). This was about 55% higher than the 6.9 MtCO2e reported in FY2025 and nearly three times the 3.6 MtCO2e recorded in FY2024. Purchased goods and services accounted for the largest share, at 9.3 MtCO2e. Capital goods added another 955,000 tonnes. These figures highlight the emissions linked to manufacturing chips, servers, and other equipment across Nvidia’s supply chain. Nvidia also reported 308,891 tonnes of location-based Scope 2 emissions in FY2026, up from 228,378 tonnes a year earlier. This measures emissions linked to the electricity mix in the regions where the company operates. The figures need some context. Nvidia is a fabless chip company, meaning it does not own the manufacturing plants that produce its chips. Much of its environmental footprint therefore comes from suppliers and other parts of its value chain. The Scope 3 total in its published emissions table covers categories 1 to 8. It should not be confused with a complete estimate of all emissions linked to the use of its sold products. Nvidia says it matched 100% of its global electricity consumption with clean electricity for sites under its operational control in FY2026. It used on-site solar, power purchase agreements, renewable electricity tariffs, and energy attribute certificates to meet this goal. However, this does not mean all its facilities physically run on renewable power at all times. The company has also adopted two emissions targets validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi). From a fiscal 2023 baseline, it aims to: Nvidia is also promoting liquid cooling and more efficient data center designs. These technologies can reduce cooling needs and improve computing performance per unit of energy. However, total electricity demand may still rise as AI use expands. The company reported about 1.05 million megawatt-hours of energy consumption in FY2026, up from 816,000 MWh a year earlier. It also reported 451,297 cubic meters of water withdrawal, although changes in data collection limit comparisons with previous years. The International Energy Agency has warned that growing data center demand will put more pressure on power systems. This makes cleaner electricity, stronger grids, and better energy efficiency increasingly important. Nvidia’s latest earnings show that the AI boom continues to generate exceptional revenue and profits. Its strong outlook also suggests that demand for AI chips and data center systems could remain high. However, rising Scope 3 emissions show the environmental cost of this growth. Matching operational electricity use with clean energy and improving chip efficiency are important steps, but they do not fully address emissions from manufacturing and the wider AI supply chain. Nvidia’s FY2030 targets provide a framework for tracking progress. The bigger test will be whether the company and its suppliers can reduce emissions as production and AI infrastructure continue to expand. Its leadership transition adds another challenge as the company works to maintain its growth and manage the environmental impact of the AI industry it helps power. Its semiconductors are the gold standard; it's involved in a lot of AI financing; and CUDA, its programming platform, is the go-to for millions of developers. Those are parts of Nvidia's business that'll flourish with or without Huang. Interim CEO Colette Kress inherited a tale of two companies. On one hand, Nvidia is currently one of the world's most important companies and has tons of resources. If you're interested in Nvidia stock, the main reason to buy it at whatever price it's trading at when you're ready is that you don't want to time the market. Trying to is essentially like gambling. title: NVIDIA (NVDA) Q3 2027 Earnings Call Transcript - The Motley Fool
content: Record $115.8 billion quarter as Vera Rubin ramped and leadership changed. By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 18, 2026 at 10:08AM EST Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email pr@fool.com NVIDIA (NVDA -3.30%) reported total revenue of $115.8 billion for the third quarter and announced a leadership transition following the resignation of its long-term chief executive. Management raised the fiscal year 2028 revenue growth guidance to approximately 75% and reported that the Vera Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in its first quarter of production shipments. The company is expanding its global supply chain through new advanced packaging and substrate agreements with Kinsus, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and SPIL to address sustained demand for AI infrastructure. Additionally, NVIDIA announced a definitive agreement to acquire Hugging Face and established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee to manage engagement with the U.S. government. Operator: Good afternoon. My name is Sarah, and I will be your conference operator today. At this time, I would like to welcome everyone to NVIDIA's Third Quarter Financial Results Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Thank you. Toshiya Hari, you may begin your conference. Toshiya Hari: Thank you. Good afternoon, and welcome to NVIDIA's conference call for the third quarter of fiscal 2027. With me today from NVIDIA are Colette Kress, Interim Chief Executive Officer and Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer; and Harvey Jones, Chairman of the Board. Our call is being webcast live on NVIDIA's Investor Relations website. The webcast will be available for replay until the conference call to discuss our financial results for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027. The content of today's call is NVIDIA's property. It can't be reproduced or transcribed without our prior written consent. During this call, we may make forward-looking statements based on current expectations. These are subject to a number of significant risks and uncertainties, and our actual results may differ materially. For a discussion of factors that could affect our future financial results and business, please refer to the disclosure in today's earnings release, our most recent Forms 10-K and 10-Q, and the reports that we may file on Form 8-K with the Securities and Exchange Commission. All our statements are made as of today, November 17, 2026, based on information currently available to us. Except as required by law, we assume no obligation to update any such statements. During this call, we will discuss non-GAAP financial measures. You can find a reconciliation of these non-GAAP financial measures to GAAP financial measures in our CFO commentary, which is posted on our website. With that, let me turn the call over to Harvey for some opening remarks. Harvey Jones: Thank you, Toshiya. Good afternoon, everybody, and thank you for joining us today. As Chairman of NVIDIA's Board of Directors, I want to say a few words on the Board's behalf. NVIDIA is an exceptionally strong company. Its strength comes from its extraordinary people, groundbreaking technology and exemplary track record of execution. Our financial performance speaks for itself. On November 12, our Board of Directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as President, CEO and Board member. The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO. The Board appointed Colette Kress, NVIDIA's longtime and well-respected CFO, as Interim CEO. In addition, the Board announced it was initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive, and we have since retained Heidrick & Struggles to lead the search. While this was an unexpected transition, the Board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners and shareholders. This morning, the company announced that our Board has established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee that will include a select group of our independent Board of Directors, senior external advisers and legal counsel. This committee will enhance our engagement with the U.S. government, including all relevant agencies. We will not be addressing or taking questions on today's call regarding the circumstances of Jensen's resignation and the ongoing investigation. Our Board will communicate further when appropriate. On behalf of our shareholders, the Board is proactively dealing with the immediate consequences facing the company as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward. We have an incredibly talented leadership team, and we have every confidence in Colette's leadership, integrity and ability to deliver as interim CEO. Colette has been at the center of this company's extraordinary growth for the last 13 years, instrumental in executing strategy and with a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position. The Board and the entire leadership team remain laser-focused on driving NVIDIA forward. Our commitment to generating value for shareholders, customers and partners remains unchanged. With that, I will turn it over to Colette. Colette Kress: Thank you, Harvey. Our momentum is real. With the market-leading multiyear road map, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate NVIDIA's leadership position. Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. And our commitment to customers, partners and shareholders will not change. Now let me transition to our financials. We delivered another outstanding quarter, marked by record revenue, operating income and EPS. Total revenue of $116 billion, more than doubled year-over-year and grew 20% on a sequential basis. Vera Rubin is off to an extraordinary start. In its first quarter of production shipments, the Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue, making it the fastest product ramp in NVIDIA's history. We're addressing strong demand for compute across a diverse and expansive set of end customers, including hyperscalers, frontier labs, AI natives, enterprises and governments. This, combined with increased support from our supply base, we are raising our fiscal year 2028 outlook. We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year-over-year, up from 70% and off what is now a higher fiscal 2027 base. Our outlook considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand and our customers' access to capital. Q3 Data Center revenue increased 21% quarter-over-quarter to $108 billion with balanced growth across hyperscale and AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise subsegments. Hyperscale revenue of $60 billion grew 23% sequentially, driven by the Vera Rubin ramp and sustained strength in Grace Blackwell. Our hyperscale customers' cloud revenue growth accelerated for the sixth consecutive quarter. Cloud industry backlog now sits at $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just 3 months ago, underscoring the significant multiyear opportunity ahead of our partners and of NVIDIA. Proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic continue to advance the frontier with OpenAI launching its latest GPT-6 models and Anthropic releasing its Claude 5.5 models. As frontier models become more capable, adoption and revenue are scaling rapidly with Anthropic's annualized revenue reaching $81 billion at the end of October. We expect the major frontier labs to contribute approximately 15% of our Data Center revenue this year. Open models are accelerating. AI adoption and weekly token volume on OpenRouter has surged 35x year-over-year and 3.5x in just this past 3 months. Agentic workloads now account for approximately 80% of tokens. A rapidly expanding ecosystem of inference providers is bringing these models to companies everywhere. At NVIDIA, we are committed to fostering a vibrant open model ecosystem so every country, company and industry can build its own intelligence. In September, we entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Hugging Face, the home of open model community, serving more than 18 million developers and 200,000 companies. Together, we will scale its platform and make intelligence more open, more capable and more accessible. Nemotron is now the most widely used U.S. open model on OpenRouter and is where developers start to build their own intelligence. That foundation is empowering the ecosystem. This past quarter, leading enterprise software and security companies, including Microsoft, Salesforce, Palantir, CrowdStrike, Cadence and Synopsys announced products that use posttrained open models tailored to domain-specific use cases. Training partners such as Scale, Mercor, Prime Intellect and Applied Compute are helping enterprises turn open models into their own using their data, tools and workflows and start-ups across specialized domains, including Lila Sciences, Harvey, Therna and Abridge, are using posttrained open models to deliver results in science, law and health care. All of this is creating a powerful flywheel. Token prices have fallen nearly 60% since May, accelerating token usage and demand for compute. As a result, GPU rental prices are rising across generations. Hopper GPUs have recontracted at up to twice their original price under the multiyear agreements, while the B300 rates have risen more than 60% since their introduction. NVIDIA compute remains fully utilized across every hyperscaler and neocloud we serve, underscoring the productivity, durability and fungibility of our infrastructure. As agents run longer and act with greater autonomy, organizations need stronger controls to ensure safety and security. The NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, which we announced alongside more than 100 partners, enables these controls. OpenShell contains agents by limiting their access to files and tools, while NVIDIA Sentry running on BlueField-4 monitors the behavior in silicon and stops agents from overstepping limits in milliseconds. OpenShell is already gaining broad ecosystem support from partners across AI models, enterprise software, cybersecurity, cloud infrastructure and robotics. Companies working with NVIDIA include Anthropic, AWS, CoreWeave, CrowdStrike, Dell, Google Cloud, HPE, IREN, JPMorgan Chase, Lenovo, Microsoft, Nebius, OpenAI and SpaceXSI. Advances in agent harnesses are accelerating the adoption of agentic AI. Meta's Muse agent launched on NVIDIA's infrastructure surpassed 10 million setups in the United States and Canada within the first 6 weeks. To support this massive scale and future growth, Meta extends (sic) [ intends ] to expand its deployment of Vera Rubin hardware with the goal of maximizing performance and efficiency for its next generation of AI agents. Agentic AI is driving extraordinary demand for CPUs, far outstripping supply. NVIDIA Vera CPU meets the growing demand, delivering leading performance at data center processing and scientific simulation workloads. CoreWeave, Meta, Nscale and OpenAI have now adopted Vera, joining AWS, OCI and SpaceXSI, the leading partners we announced last quarter. We continue to see very strong demand for Vera and expect total CPU revenue to more than double in fiscal year '28. AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise or ACI&E revenue of $47 billion increased 18% sequentially and nearly tripled year-over-year. Sequential growth was driven by Vera Rubin shipments to top leading neocloud customers and the start of our frontier labs building their own data centers. Neoclouds remain an increasingly important part of the global AI infrastructure ecosystem, providing additional customers with access to NVIDIA compute and expanding the reach of our platform. We have supported the development of this ecosystem, and we will continue to be disciplined and selective in our support. NVIDIA's full stack AI technology platform uniquely positions us to address opportunities across sovereign, enterprise and physical AI. Sovereign AI revenue more than tripled year-over-year in Q3. In September, we announced a collaboration with multiple NVIDIA cloud partners in Australia to develop up a 2 gigawatts of land, power and shell capacity by the end of calendar '27 with an opportunity to host multiple generations of NVIDIA DSX AI factories. In enterprise, financial services delivered the strongest growth with on-prem revenue reaching nearly $5 billion on a trailing 12-month basis and more than doubled year-over-year as more customers leverage NVIDIA infrastructure to accelerate quantitative trading. We expect enterprise revenue to be more than double in fiscal year '28. Physical AI revenue nearly tripled year-over-year in Q3 and is now on track to exceed $25 billion for the full year. At GTC Berlin, we expanded our NVIDIA Isaac robotics platform with a new humanoid reference design built on Isaac GR00T and Jetson Thor. In automotive, NVIDIA Hyperion and Alpamayo are enabling Mercedes-Benz and Bolt with Lucid to build robotaxi fleets, Einride to develop Level 4 autonomous trucks and Volvo Cars to advance safe, automated driving. Q3 Edge Computing revenue of $8.2 billion increased 14% sequentially and 42% year-over-year. Sequential growth was driven by stronger enterprise demand for Blackwell workstations and edge compute for physical AI applications. Q3 sales of licensed Hopper Data Center products to China was $2.4 billion. Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper Data Center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper Data Center products to China. Transitioning to an update on our supply chain, financial commitments and guarantees. Expanding our global supply chain to support customers' growth remains a top priority. With demand continuing to outpace supply, we are working closely with our partners to accelerate capacity expansion across critical components, including wafers, substrates and advanced packaging. Today, we are announcing new agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics in substrates and SPIL in advanced packaging, further strengthening our global supply chain capacity and resiliency. These build on partnerships we announced last month with Amkor, IBIDEN, KYEC and Unimicron. In Q3, our purchase commitments increased to $390 billion, reflecting our confidence in the long-term sustainability of demand for NVIDIA infrastructure. We are securing data center and cloud capacity required to support our R&D efforts across hardware and software and increasingly in open models. Together, our data center lease and cloud service commitments increased to a little over $100 billion, driven primarily by our long-term leases. Commitments associated with our neocloud agreements totaled $32 billion at the end of Q3. Under these agreements, we earn revenue from the upfront sale of our infrastructure and participate in upside in rental revenue above a minimum commitment. Total guarantees were $118 billion at the end of Q3, including the $105 billion in credit support for land, power and shell capacity for the PORTS-Pike campus we discussed last quarter. The site will exclusively host NVIDIA infrastructure under a 20-year leases to OpenAI. SoftBank Energy plans are on track with capacity expected to come online in phases beginning in calendar 2028. We continue to work closely with our infrastructure capital partners to stand up the financing platforms. These partners are instrumental in financing the build-out of AI infrastructure. As we advance this work, we remain thoughtful in how we participate and disciplined in how we commit capital. We are proud of the role that we have played so far in supporting the ecosystem. As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments and guarantees. NVIDIA's ability to extreme co-design across compute, networking, systems, algorithms and software are unmatched, driving the X-factor leaps in performance per watt and per dollar on an annual cadence. On the MLPerf Endpoints benchmark, Vera Rubin delivered 10x more tokens per watt over GB300. With Vera Rubin still early in its life cycle, we expect continuous software optimization to deliver even greater performance over time. The transition from Grace Blackwell to Vera Rubin has been exceptionally smooth. Just 3 months after we began production shipments in August, production ramps are landing in data centers at every major hyperscaler and leading neoclouds. Our hyperscale partners brought Vera Rubin into production in about 1 month, in half the time required with Grace Blackwell. Our networking franchise continues to scale with Q3 revenue exceeding $21 billion. Our co-packaged optics road map remains on track with CPO scale-out in volume production. At Supercomputing '26, Lambda announced the first production deployment of NVIDIA Photonics CPO switches, connecting more than 10,000 GB300 GPUs. Compared with pluggable optics, NVIDIA Photonics switches delivered 5x better power efficiency, 15x higher reliability and 10% lower latency. We remain on track to launch Vera Rubin Ultra next year and Feynman in 2028. The next big leap is on the horizon. At GTC Berlin, we introduced DSX POD, a full stack modular AI factory reference architecture. Just as Grace Blackwell NVL72 moved rack assembly from the data center into the supply chain, DSX POD extends that approach to the entire cluster. Pods arrive ready to connect, cutting deployment times from months to weeks, accelerating time to first token with annual revenue generating from 1 gigawatt AI factory approaching $50 billion, reaching first token just 1 quarter earlier could generate more than $10 billion in additional revenue for the operator. We are working more than a dozen partners, including Dell, Foxconn, Schneider Electric and Vertiv. We plan to ship our first pods to customers in the U.S. and Central Europe early next year. I'm going to move to the rest of the P&L. GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins were 74.8% and 74.9% and exceeded our guidance due to better product mix. GAAP and non-GAAP operating expenses were up 9% and 7% sequentially, respectively, on higher compute and infrastructure spend. Operating expenses came in marginally below our outlook, primarily due to the timing of NRE expenses. Our non-GAAP effective tax rate of 17% increased from a year ago, primarily due to higher revenue. In Q3, we returned a record $28 billion to shareholders, $22 billion through share repurchases and $6 billion in cash dividends. We have returned 65% of free cash flow on a year-to-date basis. And going forward, we intend to return all excess free cash flow, net of strategic uses, to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward. During the quarter, we authorized an additional $150 billion increase to our share repurchase program, the largest in history, and we exited Q3 with $227 billion remaining under our authorization. We continue to plan to execute our buyback authorization by the end of fiscal 2028. Now let me turn to the outlook for the fourth quarter. Please note, we will have an additional week in Q4. Total revenue is expected to be $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. We expect sequential growth to be driven by robust demand for AI infrastructure and the continued ramp of Vera Rubin. New export controls were released by the U.S. Commerce Department this week. However, with demand far exceeding supply, we expect our performance to remain strong. As mentioned earlier, we now expect fiscal 2028 revenue to grow approximately 75% off what is now a higher fiscal '27 base. GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins are expected to be between 71% and 72%, consistent with the outlook we provided last quarter. We expect Q4 to mark the bottom of gross margins before improving to the 72% to 73% range in fiscal year '28. GAAP and non-GAAP operating expenses are expected to be approximately $11 billion and $10.7 billion, respectively, impacted by the additional week and transition-related costs. We will continue to prioritize investments that support market growth and further strengthen our market position. For full year fiscal 2027, we continue to expect GAAP and non-GAAP tax rates to be between 16% and 18%, excluding any discrete items and material changes to our tax environment. Finally, we plan to file our 10-Q in the coming weeks. In the interim, we have provided a supplemental document with additional financial information on our investor website. Toshiya Hari: Thank you, Colette. We will now transition to Q&A. Ian Buck, Vice President of Hyperscale and High Performance Computing, will be joining Colette to answer your questions. Operator, please poll for questions. Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from Joseph Moore with Morgan Stanley. Joseph Moore: Great. I wonder if you could talk about the next year outlook for 75% growth. I know you were constrained, largely wafers, but there were other constraints as well. What gives you the confidence to raise that number? And do you still feel like -- you said that demand is going to be stronger than that number. At one point, you talked about 100% with the new BIS rules. Do you still think that, that 100% is kind of the right way to think about demand? Colette Kress: Yes. Thank you, Joe, for the question. That is correct. We are looking into our next fiscal year. We had originally indicated that we would be at about 70% growth year-over-year, and now we are increasing that to 75% growth. We took a lot of time working into both our demand that continues to be growing as well as our additional supply that we are able to provide to our different customers. Those 2 things together continue to give us more and more growth opportunity for us. Additionally, we did look at an assessment in terms of the current export controls. We're still going to spend some time studying those to see the different pieces of it. But we feel confident in terms of both the demand that we have in front of us as well as the supply and additional supply that we can do the 75%. Operator: Your next question comes from Vivek Arya with Bank of America Securities. Vivek Arya: Colette, I appreciate that some decisions are still evolving, but I'm curious, what is your message to NVIDIA investors about just the structural moats and the talent retention at the company. What kind of remains durable? What could change during this leadership transition? Just how do you and the Board envision the company's competitive positioning and the financial strategy as you work through this leadership transition? Colette Kress: Let me see if I will start, and I'll have Harvey see if he could say a few words as well. Probably the most important thing that we think through right now is our employees. Our employees are absolutely important, instrumental to everything in this company. We are always thinking about our employees. Like every community that there is out there, there are diverse opinions. Our employees, though, we believe, are committed. They are committed to doing their life's work at NVIDIA, and that has been true about our company from the very beginning. We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and making sure the work can be done in the current environment. I think there's also a time to think about our leadership and how important our leadership is across this organization. Our leadership has stood up so strongly over the last week to support both what we are doing here at earnings, but also supporting all of our different employees around the world. Supporting them and moving to work their jobs in every single day as they always do is what I highly understand them to do always. But honestly, they have been even greater than that in terms of the work -- working seamlessly in terms of what we need to complete. Remember, we have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multiyear road map, and I think that's important. From a business perspective, it's business as usual. We've engaged with our customers. We've engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They're all 100% up behind us. Customers have expressed their support to the business outlook and helping us through that. They've been working closely with our suppliers to narrow the supply and demand gaps as well. And I see right now the leadership even from TSMC that was in our offices just this week, also fully engaged in helping us. We've secured memory. We've secured advanced packaging. But I think the most important thing is where we are internally as a company and the strength that we have to continue. And I'll turn it over to Harvey to see if he has more. Harvey Jones: I think Colette said it very well. From the Board's point of view, we take the search very seriously. We're going to look into internal candidates as well as external candidates. The Board appreciates that we're living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace. Our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So the search will be thorough, and we want to install the CEO, the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person. Operator: Your next question comes from Timothy Arcuri with UBS. Timothy Arcuri: Colette, I wanted to ask about this new gross margin comment that you'll be in the 72% to 73% range for calendar 2027. And I wanted to see if you can speak to your ability to kind of maintain pricing power and margins over the longer term. And I ask because if you look at the frontier model guys, they're leaning in even more aggressively on ASIC and they're talking about compute efficiency as new KPIs. Is there an acceptable rate of margin compression that you might be willing to live with to protect your competitive position given all that's going on? Colette Kress: Thanks, Tim, for the question. In our last earnings, we did discuss where we saw our gross margins, not only for the last 2 quarters of fiscal year '27, but we also gave an outlook in terms of fiscal year '28. If you recall at the time, there was a significant change in terms of the cost of supply throughout the quarter that we were in as well as what we were going to move in terms of fiscal year '28. So it was important for us to rework in what we thought would be important. Yes, we thought about in terms of our prices and pieces of that and a lot of the costs were some of the things that we absorbed in those numbers that we included. What we provided here in Q4 is our bottom. If you recall, that was our bottom as we honored many of the different POs that we had already received from our customers, and we just wanted to make sure that, that was held solid as we move to a new pricing as we moved into the new year. Your statement regarding the changes that we are making. Those changes regarding fiscal year '28 are in line with what we communicated last quarter that we see in fiscal year '28. We see no changes at this time. We feel confident in terms of those numbers that we will be able to do. For the long term and our thoughts in terms of pricing going forward, remember, when you think about our full road map and our systems, probably one of the most important parts is they are very, very world-class. And everything that we enable within those systems is so important. But again, it drives such an important piece of the work that is completed. And I think our pricing is well thought through, but that is something for the future, we'll continue to think through what that pricing might be. Operator: Your next question comes from C.J. Muse with Cantor Fitzgerald. Christopher Muse: ACIE is a very important growth vector for NVIDIA. I'm hoping you could update us on your appetite for future vendor financing. And if there is any change here, what are the implications for growth for this important segment, particularly for your NCP customers? Colette Kress: Thanks for the question, C.J. So let's kind of break down that group of folks that are in that AI&E (sic) [ ACI&E ] piece of it. One of the more important areas are always together. And one of those is going to be, yes, our neoclouds. Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world, particularly on the sovereign perspective. And we continue to be working with them. But always remember, there's also other different types of groups within that category as well. We spend a lot in terms of where we are shipping in terms of our enterprises customers. Our enterprises and building their AI factories has been important for them and the neoclouds enable them to essentially have a private cloud for them to complete that. We've also seen in terms of many of our physical AI and others that are working in terms of that piece as well. So our Edge Computing can sometimes also just have Data Center help included in that. So we actually have a vast group of different types of customers that are within that group to watch. Now how do we think about in terms of the future and potential financing that will be necessary? The most important part of the financing that we would probably review but have to review in detail to make sure it is the right thing is focusing on land, power, shell. The availability of land, power, shell is such a critical part of the whole structure in terms of building out those data centers. So they may need the assistance. That's a great asset for anyone to hold. So we will look at that as probably one of our top priorities. We -- as you heard in our announcement here that we've been discussing about many of our financing funds that have been helping us, and they can be a very big part of that work as well in terms of the neoclouds or even any of the enterprises in the work that they want to do. We have a strong amount of companies that we work with that are not only working in terms of in enterprises or in big businesses, but keep in mind, they are also IG customers. Those IG customers can be very helpful, particularly when it comes to enabling the amount of money that is required. We can look at them in terms of the assistance of meeting in terms of prepaying, which can help in terms of their build of that data center. So right now, I think we would look at this and taking a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing as a lot of things have changed over this last quarter, and we know that's a priority of ours, but we do have some very, very strong existing customers that we will be continuing to work with. Operator: Your next question comes from Stacy Rasgon with Bernstein Research. Stacy Rasgon: Colette, I wanted to follow up on that. In the CFO commentary, it looks to me a new sentence or new paragraph on the neoclouds. It says your commitments take effect only if the neoclouds secure financing to purchase the data center infrastructure products and related compute capacity deployed. Maximum commitment, blah, blah, blah. And it says certain commitments may be reduced or eliminated if they don't do this. I guess I'm asking, is this -- it's a new sentence in the CFO disclosure. Is this something new in how you're doing business with the neoclouds? Or is this something that you've been doing all along and you're just telling us about it now? Because it sounds like you guys are not the ones that are actually looking to provide the financing. It reads like they have to secure their own financing in order to get the backstops and commitments from you. Colette Kress: Thanks, Stacy, for the question. Let me see if I can clarify for everyone about what that means. When we are looking at many of our different types of guarantees, much of the land, power, shell that has to be built and put together, there is construction, there is the raising of capital that they may need through equity and/or debt in order to build out any of the buildings, get them ready for use, but also the ability to procure the compute, install the compute and get ready. What we are indicating in our statement there is that is when our guarantee starts. So if all of that begins and unfortunately, they are delayed or they have a challenge in terms of building that, our guarantee doesn't exist anymore. Our guarantee for most of these are really about when they are ready to go, particularly when we think about our one in terms of Portsmouth in terms of what we could do. These are important things to understand because that shows what we have done in terms of really thoughts in terms of very, very strong businesses that we felt could actually maintain creating the debt and equity that they needed to get that done and create the data center such that we felt very confident in terms of that guarantee. Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No. What this is only saying is that we wanted to make sure that the clarity, there was other communication in another part that would have already communicated this, but we just wanted to make sure it was very clear as we had been receiving some of the questions on how that exactly worked. Operator: Your next question comes from Ben Reitzes with Melius Research. Benjamin Reitzes: Nice presentation tonight, Colette and team. I wanted to ask about if you could give me any idea on what you think about this idea that there needs to be a big slowdown in 2028 due to the change in government and some of the policies that we may see. There's obviously -- I'm sure you're aware of the big fears that there could be a slowdown after your great calendar '27. Is there something that you're seeing increased confidence in this? Have you spoken to anyone in the administration or not administration, but in government since the blue wave? And anything that gives you confidence beyond '27 that you might want -- might be able to tell us about? Colette Kress: Yes. So thanks, Ben, for the question. Where we stand right now, there is so much demand with such the largest companies continuing to work on so many agentic solutions, new models that are also available. And that's been our focus to assist. I'd say even in the last week, the continued ask, how are we going to receive more and more supply to help them with the demand that they have in front of them? So they're all getting ready for that. I know there's been a lot of focus in terms of the data centers within the United States as well. Are they well positioned to take care of the communities that are around that? And I think that's very important that all companies are working together so that the communities understand both the jobs that are going to be newly available, but giving them the confidence regarding how they will be perceived and working within those areas as well. So I think that is an area to focus on, but I think there is a lot of data centers already in use or ready to go that might be that case. We're always going to be engaged with the government, making sure that we are all aligned in terms of what we see in terms of the future. But I think the demand and what we have in terms of agentic will continue not only in the '27 perspective, but moving to the '28 as well as we'll continue to carry over the amount of demand that's in front of us. Operator: Your next question comes from Joshua Buchalter with TD Cowen. Joshua Buchalter: I want to offer a sincere good luck to you and the employees during this transition. In the prepared remarks, you were clear that demand continues to meaningfully outstrip supply. But should we expect any changes to how NVIDIA allocates its available capacity across the key buckets of end demand like hyperscalers, AI labs and neoclouds? You mentioned that AI labs are likely to be about 15% of revenue this year, which is, I think, roughly flat with some disclosures you gave over the summer. But how big could that bucket be, for instance, over time? Colette Kress: Thanks for the question. So when we think about our allocation, we do think about very important parts that we need to understand to make sure that in the quarter that we need to ship, they will be able to use and use very efficiently in the very beginning. What that means is that land, power, shell, whether or not it's structured, ready to go, is already set up and completed to do so. That's one of the most important things. The second thing, though, is also to think about their capital needs. Their capital, it needs to be set up, ready to go for us to work in terms of that allocation. Many of our customers outside of the IG will want to provide and think through in terms of their offtake as we will be needing an understanding of do they have that solid offtake that they will be able to run as well. So our allocation runs from we're here for everyone, particularly when there is already a PO available, and we feel those means in terms of capital will happen, and we will continue to be allocating as quickly as possible when we know the amount of supply that we will think we will have. So I believe this is a process that will continue to grow as more supply comes in. We'll continue working in terms of more allocation. But right now, that's probably the best way that I would describe all of our process that we are doing. It is not anything in terms of any types of different pricing. All are getting the same pricing that is super important for us, and we just need to assure that they are ready on their side in terms of being able to accept the compute. It sounds like there's no change to your existing commitments to partners or supply chain partners or customers, and you've reiterated the buyback commentary you talked about previously. Can you maybe just kind of clarify whether there is anything about the hurdle rates or thresholds for customer financing specifically that is changing going forward? Or is that unchanged? And can you maybe also address the timing or relative sequencing of buybacks versus customer financing or the partner financing? Colette Kress: Okay. So let me clarify for you, Jim, where we stand in terms of returning capital to shareholders. Super top priority for us, first and foremost, to understand. We already are with the $150 billion increase in our opportunity. It is going to be used and hopefully, in terms of fully used for the full fiscal year '28. And that is going to be something that we want to do, and we believe we have the capability to do so. But equally, there are important areas that we need to keep in mind for the capital use. The top priority is going to be our suppliers. Our suppliers are working feverishly to build more demand for us. And some of that demand needs assistance -- excuse me, some of that supply needs assistance in terms of capital from any forms of different types of prepaids to help them in terms of capacity. We want to make sure that we're there for them so they can move as quickly as possible. I think that is a very great use of our capital to help support that part of it. Additionally, there are areas where we will see some of our expected committed investments that we need to make that we may need to finish. Not a very large piece of it, but something that we need to do. When you think about just on the edge of a set of types of very strong customers that may need assistance in terms of financing of some type of guarantee, that is something we will do. It is a process that we will look very deeply in terms of the company, the strength of what they have planned as well as everything that they need in terms of that data center to do so. So there will be a portion that we will do. But again, something other -- a lot of work to understand if those are the right types of investments that we need to make. So thinking about all of that together, I think there is definitely the room to continue all of the stock repurchases plans that we want to do and complete those before the end of fiscal year '28. The Santa Clara chip giant said it was looking for a replacement for the former chief executive and declined to answer questions about Huang during a conference call after its latest earnings report on Tuesday. Nvidia's leadership has been in flux after Huang resigned and admitted to an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. Other affairs, including with an Nvidia employee, have surfaced since. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia's chairman, said in an opening statement. "While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders." The company's stance came amid growing calls to hire back Jensen. Jensen himself said this week that he would be willing to return as CEO if the board invited him back. "Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang wrote in an X post. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." The company reported record profits of $116 billion for the quarter that ended in September, doubling from last year. The revenue beat analyst expectations of $109 billion, reinforcing the strong demand for AI applications. It raised its growth outlook for the coming quarter and year. Nvidia shares, which have tumbled 20% so far this year, climbed around 4% in after-hours trading Tuesday after the earnings announcement. The stock price was near $160 in early after-hours trading. "The tone of the call sent the message that Nvidia is moving forward without Jensen Huang without saying so explicitly," said Jacob Bourne, analyst at Emarketer. "Interim CEO Colette Kress led that message, projecting optimism, confidence, and a clear sense of direction for the company's future." The board has launched an investigation into Huang's affair and said it does not believe Huang divulged Nvidia secrets or compromised national security. The board appointed longtime Chief Financial Officer Kress as interim chief executive. In response to a surge in security concerns, the Nvidia board said Tuesday that it has formed a committee to oversee compliance with national security and export controls for its advanced chips, a focus that has come into sharp relief in Washington. "This committee will enhance our engagement with the U.S. government, including all relevant agencies," Jones said. Huang is a central figure of the AI boom, whose advanced semiconductor chips underpin 90% of the global market. Through savvy dealmaking and by bankrolling smaller startups, he turned Nvidia into a $5-trillion colossus. This created an extremely loyal employee base, many of whom want him to return, increasing pressure on the new management to ease fears and prevent potential employee churn. "We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and making sure the work can be done in the current environment," Kress said. Huang advocated relaxing export controls on advanced chips to China, arguing that cutting off access would only accelerate China's resolve to build domestic alternatives. He leveraged his relationship to President Trump to overturn a Biden-era export ban and sold less powerful chips to Chinese customers, in exchange for a percentage of sales revenue going to the U.S. government. Nvidia has lost nearly $2 trillion in market value since his departure. Over the weekend, Huang's allies in Silicon Valley started a "Stand with Jensen," campaign demanding his return. The letter received over 100,000 signatures, including from employees, and support from Tesla Chief Executive Elon Musk. Trump also reposed his faith in Huang since the affair first surfaced, and earlier this week said that he "would not mind" if he returned.
